title: The Rupee Just Posted Its First Quarterly Gain Since March 2025 — Here's What Changed and What NRI Investors Should Watch Next
excerpt: Oil's 42% crash from $126 to $73, a barrage of RBI measures, and $2.4 billion in net foreign inflows helped the rupee recover from record lows near 97 to settle around 94.66 — but the Fed's hawkish tilt and a weak monsoon cloud the outlook.
body:
On the last trading day of June, the Indian rupee closed at 94.66 against the dollar — down slightly on the session, but up roughly 0.2 per cent for the quarter. That modest number belies one of the most dramatic turnarounds in recent Indian currency history.

This is the rupee's first quarter-on-quarter gain since March 2025, snapping a run of four consecutive quarters of decline that at one point drove the currency to record lows near 97 to the dollar in May. For NRI investors and remitters, the shift is more than academic: it affects the real value of every dollar converted into rupees, every SIP denominated in Indian equities, and every NRE deposit sitting in an Indian bank account.

## What Drove the Recovery

Three forces converged to rescue the rupee from its worst levels.

**The oil price collapse.** Brent crude, which spiked above $126 a barrel in April during the Iran conflict, has crashed 42 per cent to trade near $73. India's crude oil basket averaged $83.85 per barrel in June, down sharply from $114.48 in April and $106.23 in March. For an economy that imports over 80 per cent of its oil, this single variable drives the current account deficit, the inflation outlook, and by extension, the rupee.

**RBI's policy salvo.** The Reserve Bank of India didn't wait for the rupee to recover on its own. It extended a subsidised forex swap facility for banks' overseas borrowings, allowed commercial banks to lend to non-residents against foreign-currency deposits, and continued offering FCNR deposits at up to 7.5 per cent to attract NRI dollar inflows. FX reserves have started rebuilding, rising to $672.59 billion in the week ended June 19 after months of depletion from intervention.

**The return of foreign capital.** Net FPI inflows hit nearly $2.4 billion in the last week of June alone, reversing months of outflows and taking cumulative June investment to about $531 million. Foreign investors also poured a record $3 billion into Indian government bonds in June, attracted by tax incentives and expanded bond market access.

## The Market Scorecard: June Winners and Losers

Indian benchmarks closed the month of June with gains — the Sensex up 2.3 per cent and the Nifty 50 up 1.4 per cent — despite Tuesday's session ending in the red on derivative expiry jitters and IT sector weakness.

**Winners:** Banking and financial stocks led convincingly. The Nifty Bank index rose 6.1 per cent in June, private banks gained 6.1 per cent, public sector banks 4.1 per cent, and financials 4.7 per cent. Pharma added 4 per cent. Broader small-caps surged 4 per cent.

**Losers:** IT was the clear casualty, with the Nifty IT index falling 9.6 per cent in June — its worst monthly performance in years. The drag came from two directions: rising US inflation expectations fuelling fears of Fed rate hikes (which would crimp client IT spending), and Accenture's weak demand forecast amplified by broader AI disruption fears. Metals dropped 6.9 per cent as Mideast supply fears receded.

## Goldman Sachs Upgrades India's Outlook

In a note that moved markets, Goldman Sachs raised its 2026 growth forecast for India by 30 basis points, lowered its inflation projection by 20 basis points, and now expects the country to log a balance of payments surplus of 0.7 per cent of GDP. The upgrade reflects the improved oil-and-currency backdrop, though analysts cautioned that the Federal Reserve's hawkish bias and India's weakest monsoon in 11 years remain live risks.

Commerzbank analysts echoed the sentiment, projecting the rupee to consolidate between 94 and 96, with potential to drop to the 92–94 range if oil prices fall further.

## What NRI Investors Should Watch in Q2

**The Fed's next move.** Fed Chair Kevin Warsh speaks Wednesday, and US labour data drops later this week. Expectations of tighter monetary policy in the US — driven by war-fuelled inflation — have kept the dollar index elevated near 101.3. A hawkish Fed limits the rupee's upside even as India's domestic factors improve.

**The monsoon.** June rainfall is running at a 43 per cent deficit. Only a meaningful pickup in July can revive optimism for rural demand, food inflation, and sectors like autos, consumer goods, and tractors. A potential super El Niño later this year remains the tail risk no one wants to discuss.

**Fuel deregulation.** From July 1, India lifts restrictions on the sale of petrol and diesel, ending measures introduced during the West Asia conflict to prevent local shortages. The move signals confidence that global supply chains have stabilised — but any fresh disruption in the Strait of Hormuz could force a reversal.

**The FCNR window.** The RBI's enhanced FCNR deposit scheme, offering NRIs dollar deposits at up to 7.5 per cent with zero currency risk, remains open through September 2026. With the rupee stabilising, locking in these rates while they last may be one of the most attractive low-risk opportunities for diaspora investors this year.

## The Bottom Line

The rupee's quarterly gain is more symbol than substance — 0.2 per cent won't change anyone's financial plan. But the reversal in direction, after a painful stretch that saw the currency hit all-time lows, signals that the worst of the oil-driven crisis may be behind India. For NRI investors, the combination of falling oil, policy support, and renewed foreign inflows creates a cautiously favourable environment — provided the monsoon cooperates and the Fed doesn't surprise on the hawkish side.
